steps.explain: Anyone who can read the Secret object can read the password. base64 is an *encoding* for binary-safe transport, not encryption.

steps.title: What actually protects a Secret
body: base64 hides nothing. What makes Secrets safer than ConfigMaps is everything around them:
- **RBAC**: grant `get` on `secrets` to as few people and service accounts as possible. `list` secrets is effectively "read every password in the namespace".
- **Encryption at rest**: configure the API server to encrypt Secrets in etcd (managed clusters do this, often with a cloud KMS key).
- Kubelets only receive Secrets for pods scheduled on their node, and keep them in memory (tmpfs) when mounted.

- **Do not commit Secret YAML to Git**. Use Sealed Secrets, SOPS, or an external store (Azure Key Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Vault) synced in by the External Secrets Operator or the Secrets Store CSI driver.

checks.name: old-password.txt has the decoded old password
checks.fail: Not the old password. `kubectl get secret db-credentials -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d`.

checks.name: the Secret holds the new password and the same username
checks.cmd: kubectl get secret db-credentials -o jsonpath='{.data.username}' | base64 -d; echo; kubectl get secret db-credentials -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d

checks.name: a fresh api pod has the new password
checks.cmd: kubectl rollout status deploy/api --timeout=30s >/dev/null && p=$(kubectl get pods -l app=api -o json | jq -r '[.items[] | select(.metadata.deletionTimestamp == null)] | sort_by(.metadata.creationTimestamp) | last | .metadata.name') && [ "$p" != "$(cat /opt/dojo/state/old-pod)" ] && kubectl exec $p -- printenv DB_password
checks.fail: The running `api` pod still has the old password. `kubectl rollout restart deploy/api` replaces the pods.

hints: `-o jsonpath='{.data.password}'` gives base64; `| base64 -d` decodes it. Base64 is an encoding, not encryption.
`kubectl create secret generic db-credentials --from-literal=username=shop --from-literal=password=winter-example-77 --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -` updates it in place.
Environment variables are read when a container starts: `kubectl rollout restart deploy/api`.
solution: kubectl get secret db-credentials -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d > ~/answers/old-password.txt
kubectl create secret generic db-credentials --from-literal=username=shop --from-literal=password=winter-example-77 --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -
steps.explain: Anyone who can `get` a Secret can read it: base64 is only transport encoding, which is why RBAC on Secrets (and encryption at rest, or an external secret store) matters. Values injected as environment variables are fixed when the container starts, so a rotation needs a `rollout restart`; Secrets mounted as files are updated in place by the kubelet after a short delay, which suits apps that reload.
